issues.item: Triggers: Sexual Objectification: Being looked at sexually
issues.explanation: The trigger profile mixes tactile/startle-type cues and driving-with-others cues that could fit war-zone trauma, but 'being looked at sexually' points toward a sexual-threat trauma context that is not supported elsewhere in memory, threat, or appraisal items. This specific trigger is hard to reconcile with the rest of the profile.

issues.item: Threat: Watching Others: I watch other people closely for signs that they might harm me
issues.explanation: The dominant threat items describe generalized vigilance and fear of interpersonal attack. In combination with the sexual-objectification trigger, this pulls the profile toward an interpersonal/sexual trauma formulation, whereas the memory and appraisal items do not contain corresponding themes. This creates cross-node incoherence.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Failed Role: I have failed in my most important role in life
issues.explanation: 'I have failed in my most important role in life' is not impossible, but in this profile it lacks a clear link to the other selected items. The rest of the appraisals center on unfairness, shame, and inability to trust oneself; without any role-related trauma content in memory, triggers, or threat, this item feels weakly anchored and clinically mismatched relative to the otherwise war-zone/interpersonal-danger presentation.

vignette:
Leilani was forty-six years old, a veterinarian who had spent most of her career treating companion animals in a quiet suburban practice. She had grown up in a coastal town in the Pacific Islands before moving to the United States in her twenties, and she still spoke of home with a kind of warmth that seemed to belong to another lifetime. That lifetime ended on a Tuesday afternoon three years ago, when she and her husband were visiting her cousin’s family in a region that had suddenly become a war zone. They had been caught in a market during an aerial bombardment. Leilani remembered the sound first—a whistle that grew into a roar, then the ground shaking so violently that she thought the earth itself was splitting open. She had thrown herself over her cousin’s youngest child, a boy of four, and she remembered the weight of debris raining down on her back, the smell of dust and something metallic, and the way the boy’s small body trembled beneath hers. She did not remember how they got out. That part of the memory came in fragments—a hand pulling her arm, a wall of fire, a stranger’s face covered in blood—and none of the pieces seemed to fit together in a way that made a coherent story. What she did remember, with a clarity that shamed her, was that afterward, in the relative safety of a United Nations shelter, she had been unable to stop shaking. She had been useless. She had not been able to help anyone. The feeling that she could not rely on herself had taken root that night and had never let go.

In the months that followed, Leilani returned to her work, but the world felt different. She had always been a calm presence in the examination room, steady with frightened animals and anxious owners. Now she could not sit still. She found herself scanning the waiting room constantly, noting exits, watching the hands of strangers, listening for the pitch of a voice that might precede something sudden. She became unable to relax even in her own home, which she knew was safe, but knowing did not seem to matter. Her body stayed alert. She had difficulty falling asleep because she needed to stay vigilant, and when she did sleep, the memories came like a film that played over and over, always the same fragments—the whistle, the roar, the boy’s trembling body—and she would wake with her heart pounding and a feeling of intense shame that she could not name. The shame was the worst part. She was certain that she had done something wrong, that she had failed in some fundamental way, and that what had happened to her was deeply unfair and that nothing had been done about it. No one had been held accountable. The war continued. The boy’s family had fled. Leilani was left with the memory and the certainty that she could not stop bad things from happening to anyone, least of all herself.

Her avoidance was subtle at first. She stopped driving with her husband, telling him she preferred to take her own car. She began to dread the casual touch of a colleague’s hand on her shoulder, the unexpected brush of a client’s arm as they leaned over an exam table. Loud noises became unbearable—a dropped instrument tray in the clinic would send her into a cold sweat, and she started wearing noise-canceling headphones during procedures, telling herself it was for focus. At home, she arranged the furniture so that no one could approach her from behind. She slept on the side of the bed closest to the door. She stopped attending family gatherings because the unpredictability of children running and shouting felt like too much. Her husband grew quiet and hurt, and she knew he did not understand why she flinched when he reached for her in the dark, but she could not explain it. She was certain that if she let herself relax, even for a moment, something terrible would happen again.

What finally brought Leilani to seek help was not the flashbacks or the shame or the sleeplessness, though all of those had worsened. It was a moment in the clinic when a golden retriever, frightened by a sudden noise, snapped at her hand. The bite was minor. But Leilani had frozen. She had stood there, unable to move, her ears ringing, her vision tunneling, and she had thought: I can’t even do this anymore. She had excused herself, locked the bathroom door, and wept. That evening, she told her husband that she needed to talk to someone. She was afraid of what that might mean—afraid that talking would make the memories more real, that she would be judged for her helplessness, that nothing would ever change. But she was more afraid of the alternative: a life spent bracing for a blow that had already fallen.
